speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the
consent of the house I should like to make the following motion, with the understanding that if there is any objection it may stand aa a notice. The motion is:
That on and after Monday, March 24 next, and all subsequent Mondays and Wednesdays until the end of the session, government notices of motion and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except questions and notices of motions for the production of papers and private bills on Monday.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext: I had not understood the right hon. Prime Minister to say that his motion would include both days. I thought it was intended only to take Mondays and to leave Wednesdays for the time being.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that during the last three years the average time allowed to private members has been ten days. One year it was eight days; another year it was ten days and in the third year it was eleven days. This motion would allow ten full days to private members.
Perhaps I should add that there is this year an even stronger reason why this motion should be carried than was the case in previous years. Up to the present time the government has had only two days for its business since the house opened. If we except the time taken for the discussion on the speech from the throne which took but one day or two we have had only two days devoted to government business. After all the government is entitled to some place in parliament in the matter of its legislation.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext: But may I say, Mr. Speaker, that in the old days, as I remember it, there were always two motions in connection with this taking away of the days of private members. The first motion, if my memory serves me right, would be for Wednesdays, and a couple of weeks later a motion would be made with regard to Mondays. It seems rather hard for the members who have notices of motion on the order paper to be entirely shut off after this week. I should like to suggest that the Prime Minister look up the precedents, and I think he will find that this was the customary procedure.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

speechtext:
Mr. H. J. BARBER (Fraser Valley) asked leave under standing order 31 to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the necessity for immediate action to be taken by the government to prevent the dumping of eggs from the United States and other countries upon the Canadian market.
And leave having been granted:

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move the house do adjourn.
As briefly as possible I will undertake to place before the house and the government the serious condition which exists in relation to one of our branches of agriculture; I refer to the poultry industry. This industry has developed into a very valuable one, giving employment to a large number of our people. I believe that some 250,000 Canadians are employed at the present time in this industry. Statistics supplied by the Department of Trade and Commerce show that in 1928 we had over 34,000,000 producing hens with a total production of 269,000,000 dozen eggs, valued at $84,000,000. In 1921 the total production was valued at $40,000,000 and to-day that production is valued at $84,000,000, which is proof that this industry has developed very rapidly during the last few years. The minister has drawn our attention to the fact that the per capita consumption of eggs in Canada has shown a marked increase, the domestic consumption exceeding that of any other country. This can be taken as a tribute to the high quality of the Canadian egg. Some credit for this result belongs rightly to the department, but a great deal must be given to those engaged in the industry. Through careful selection and breeding we are told that the production per hen has increased in seven years from 78 to 95 eggs and through better grading and marketing the average price received during that time has increased from 25 cents to 31 cents per dozen. According to the Bureau of Statistics, our exports last year exceeded our imports, which would lead us to believe that we are now producing sufficient eggs to supply the domestic market. This is a very important industry, one employing a large number of people; an industry producing a product of the highest quality and in sufficient quantity to supply the domestic market. This industry should receive every consideration and assistance at the hands of the government.

Importation of Eggs-Mr. Barber
I have before me a telegram received from the president of the Canadian poultry pool, but before referring to it I would like to say something regarding the organization itself. This pool came into being during May of last year, its object being to organize the poultry industry of Canada for the purpose of placing it upon a sound basis, insuring the producer, on the one hand, an adequate return for his investment and labour, and insuring to the consumer, on the other hand, a continuous and wholesome supply of eggs and egg products at reasonable cost. This organization encourages the producers to take up cooperative marketing. It also aims at the standardization of the product and the supervision of packing and marketing. It has spread to the four western provinces, and numbers within its membership provincial poultry associations in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba representing a membership of 40,000 producers and
2,000	merchant members. I would consider that organization to be sufficiently representative of the poultry industry. I am advised that a similar telegram to that which I shall read was despatched to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). This telegram reads as follows:
Would invite your attention to present import of American eggs which are now flooding our Montreal, Toronto and prairie markets. Canadian production of eggs increasing rapidly and in our opinion is now sufficient to meet consumptive demand in Canada. Further import into Canada at this time will result in the demoralization of our market to an extent that Canadian producers will not receive sufficient for their eggs to cover cost of production. Request your government to immediately take such steps as may be necessary to prevent further depression of our egg market.
That telegram was dated February 28, and was signed by Alister Forbes, the president of the Canadian poultry pood. The telegram was followed by a letter dated March 8, 1930, confirming the wire and reading as follows:
About 20,000 cases of American eggs were imported into the Montreal and Toronto markets during January and I believe a similar quantity during February. Our advices are that large quantities are still being imported. These foreign eggs now entering Canada are of the lower grades but, nevertheless, they affect very adversely the price at which our high grade Canadian eggs can be marketed. These low grade eggs have a very demoralizing effect upon our markets and are especially demoralizing at the present time, when the packing house trade is endeavouring to set the price for this season's storage pack.
It is unnecessary for me to point out to you that it is not only the actual importation of these eggs that has a demoralizing effect upon
our markets, but the threat of import is almost as demoralizing as the actual accomplishment of the fact.
I have also a statement from the same organization relating to the marketing situation:
During 1928 egg prices in Canada and the United States ruled generally firm. Prices f.o.b. western Canada were on a basis of approximately 30 cents per dozen, and the Chicago market was on a similar basis. Due to a particularly mild fall and an early winter there was a considerable increase in winter production in both Canada and the United States, and the American distributors found their stocks unduly heavy and took steps to unload. Their storage market continued very weak and tremendous losses were taken by holders of storage eggs, due to the over supply. Our Canadian market immediately reflected the situation in the United States. We did not have too many eggs in store. Our prices were not too high for Canadian consumption, but due to the fact that American eggs could be imported from Chicago to our eastern markets at a cost, including duty, of approximately 4J cents a dozen, holders of Canadian storage eggs were obliged to compete with the Chicago market with the result that eggs, which had cost our Canadian distributors 40 cents in store, had to be sold for as low as 27 cents for extras, and. in some cases later in the season, eggs which "were put away as extras were cleared at 23 cents Montreal.
These distributors refused in 1929 to buy eggs on a basis of the 1928 season claiming that they must buy eggs at a price which would show them a profit against importations of American eggs. We feel they are justified in adopting this attitude under the present tariff. It is unreasonable to expect that they will cooperate to build up a profitable market to the egg producers of Canada, if they are going to be subject to the competition of American exporters who see fit to market their eggs in Canada at prices far under their cost to themselves. It is impossible for the Canadian distributors to stay in business if they have to market eggs which cost them 40 cents for 27 cents to meet American competition.
The figures of the Bureau of Statistics show that the importation of eggs for the calendar year of 1928 amounted to 996,880 dozen in shell, and 3,029,733 pounds n.o.p. In 1929 the importation of eggs in shell amounted to 713,290 dozen, and eggs, n.o.p., 560,061 pounds. I would like to refer to the following which appears on page 11 of the 1929 report of the Minister of Agriculture:
The steady growth which has characterized the poultry industry in Canada during the past few years was continued in 1928. The increased interest displayed throughout the Dominion, and in foreign countries too, is attributed in a large measure to the recent world's poultry congress. As a result of the greater demand for stock the hatching industry is in a flourishing condition. Prices held up very well on the average although the influx of eggs from British Columbia has had a tendency to break the market in eastern

speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but may I rise to a point of order? My hon. friend has been talking for a long time and as yet he has not said a word about an egg. This motion was to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. There will be an opportunity for a debate on the budget when it is brought down.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I accept the reproof of the
Prime Minister. I started on the eggs and I will lead up to eggs again if my right hon. friend will allow me to continue for a few minutes. We must keep these eggs out of the country. We must keep other things out of the country. One question is bound up with the other. This government is seeing what Belshazzar saw. We are" trying to succeed in Canada. We are trying to produce eggs and to do things for the benefit of the whole of this country. Just look at the value of the agricultural products that are brought into Canada, and those agricultural products include eggs, of course. We are an agricultural country, and the government should be willing to assist agriculture in every way possible, but at the present time we are importing far more agricultural products from our neighbours than we are exporting to them. Is that right? It is the quintessence of folly. No government can do it and remain in power, and we are going to see, when this government takes its seat to your left, Mr. Speaker, that these conditions are remedied, and the people of Canada will thank us for it. We have a wonderful country, and why should we allow this agricultural produce from other countries to flood our market to the consternation of the people in this country who are trying to earn a living? In my district there are hundreds of returned men who have gone on the land under the soldier settlement scheme, and about the only possible thing they can do on that land is to raise poultry; and faced with the present conditions they cannot succeed. What is going to happen to them? They paid too much for their land under the prices which prevailed at that time, and I repeat, if they cannot succeed in the business of raising poultry, they cannot succeed at all. No wonder that consternation prevails among them.
I would have given figures, but as I said in my opening remarks the mover has dealt in figures so exhaustively that I feel it is not necessary for me to give any more. In conclusion, I press upon the government to take

immediate action in the best interest of Canada and in the best interest of the poultry men.

speechtext:
I wish to support the resolution. I come from a constituency where a great many returned men have gone into the poultry business, and may I say that they did so with the approval of the government, the poultry business being one branch of farming that was approved for them. Conditions in British Columbia favour the production of eggs when they cannot be satisfactorily produced in eastern Canada. We feel that as Canadians we should be entitled to the Canadian market in preference to the people of the United States. I feel very keenly on this subject because I have seen how the situation is working out. The returned men are doing their very best to make good, but are having a very difficult time of it, and I must say that this government is doing nothing at all to assist them. On the contrary, if a returned man does not pay the money which is due to the government on account of his land or stock, including poultry, his land is taken away from him. I submit that the returned men should at least be given a fair chance to make good, and they are not going to make good in the poultry business if the government refuses to take action in a situation like this. There is no doubt whatever that our market is being flooded with American eggs; I am not going into details because they have already been put on record. I submit that the government should have taken action in the matter before this. The government is to blame for the present situation having arisen. On the fourth of this month I called the attention of the government to the situation and tried to ascertain what they intended to do, but my question was ruled out of order, or, at least, I was told to put it on the order paper in the usual way, and we all know what that means. It means that it is side-tracked, and that the government will not take any immediate action. What the present situation requires is prompt action on the part of the government.
I submit that we can look at this subject from another standpoint, and that is from the standpoint of unemployment. Notwithstanding the remarks that have been made from time to time by the Prime Minister and his cabinet, there is a great deal of unemployment in this country at this time. I was present recently with a delegation that waited on the Prime Minister and the cabinet, and the matter of unemployment was then discussed.
I say that unemployment to some extent is 
due to the fact that this government does not take any action at all in circumstances like these. It is a government of inaction, not a government of action. It is time, I submit, that the government should do something, and unless something is done, and done right away, a very serious situation is going to arise. I have much pleasure in supporting the resolution.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I wish to support the resolution with reference to the egg and poultry industry. This is a very important industry, fully fifty per cent of the people of this Dominion being interested in it in one way or another. Almost every farmer in this country keeps a certain number of fowl, and sells eggs and poultry. The people of the west also sell a goodl deal of poultry to Ontario and Quebec around the Christmas season, and I think therefore that the. western members should be very much interested in this question. Tiie hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), speaking a year or two ago, stated that there were fully 250,000 people in the Dominion who made their Diving from the egg and poultry industry. Whether that figure is correct or not, I do not know, but I do know that a large number of people are interested in the production of eggs and poultry. Travelling on the railway you will notice that it is not only the farmers who are producing eggs and raising poultry, but also a large number of people in the villages and smaller towns. When you consider that the people of Canada consume more eggs per capita than any other nation in the world, you will understand how important an industry it is for this country. Only the other day I read that we consume per capita about twenty-nine to thirty dozen eggs per year, far greater number than in any other country. We can produce poultry and eggs in Canada the equal of any produced anywhere else in the world. Canadian farmers and egg and poultry producers, are quite capable of supplying the demand in this country, and one of the first things we should do is to conserve so far as possible the home market for the Canadian producer. The Canadian producer will supply that market if the prices are such as to give him a fair profit. The marketing of our domestic eggs in this country is done at present under great difficulties on account of the large importations from the United States and other parts of the world, eggs in the shell, in particular, being largely imported from the United States.
I was rather surprised to hear the statement that in the months of January and

Importation oj Eggs-Mr. Anderson (Halton)
February of this year as many eggs were imported from the United States as during the whole of the preceding two years. It shows that these importations are increasing at a tremendous rate. I noticed particularly a statement made by the Deputy Minister of Agriculture in a letter sent out to the farmers of this province, and presumably to those of the Dominion, on the 28th of February, to the effect that we had ceased to export eggs. He wanted to know the reason for this state of affairs. The explanation is that the egg producer in Canada has been driven out of the market by reason of the dumping of eggs into this country from the United States.
I think every hon. member will understand that it costs the Canadian egg producers more to produce a dozen eggs than it costs his competitor in the United States, due, of course, to our climatic conditions. Our hens are very sensitive to cold weather and stop laying. In order to ensure egg production during the winter months the hens must be comfortably housed in properly ventilated structures. There is a ventilating system manufactured in the United States which is very effective, but it costs a farmer here almost $1,000 to purchase the equipment.
During 1928 the returns from our poultry industry amounted to $106,500,000, which is a good deal more than the value of our fisheries, and represents a return to the average farmer greater than he gets from some of his coarse grains. In a word, it is an important industry and should be properly protected. In 1928 a large number of people came to Ottawa to see the government with regard to the imposition of the anti-dumping clause on imported fruits and vegetables, and also eggs. The late Mr. Robb then contended -and he brought a man from Prince Edward Island in confirmation of his statement'

that the imposition of the anti-dumping clause in 1926 and 1927 did not increase the price of eggs on the Canadian market. I think that is so. I doubt very much if the anti-dumping clause in its operation would increase the price of eggs to the Canadian consumer. But it would do this: it would protect the home market for the Canadian producer of eggs. That is the one point we want to stress. Our egg producers are asking for some redress against the dumping of eggs on their home market by their competitors in the United States. I think the former Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) made the statement that the egg producer in Canada got nothing whatever for his culls. That is simply in line with what a farmer told me when I was home last week. Under the present system of grading he had brought eggs
to the retailer in his home town, and a certain number of his eggs were rejected as culls; but he was given nothing for them. He asked me whether or not he was entitled to those culled eggs. I told him that he was, and the retailer should either hand over the culls to him or pay for them. That is a condition that should not be allowed to continue. Of course, I am not blaming the government at all for it, because I think the grading of eggs has been a good thing for the average consumer, for although it has increased the price somewhat, it has also improved the quality of the eggs. It is a question whether or not grading has increased egg production in this country; I think it has. Certainly it has given satisfaction not ony to the consumer but to the producer.
I do not want to labour the question. I think the government should take it into their serious consideration with a view to giving a little protection to this very important industry that is found and*-under normal conditions-flourishes from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not from British Columbia, but coming from an industrial centre as I do and being connected with the business world, I have some knowledge of the condition of the egg industry. I was on the Toronto market last Saturday. Let me say at once that I am not dealing in eggs, but I know those who are in touch with the egg business. To-day that business is in a deplorable condition, due to the dumping of eggs from the United States, and I heartily endorse all that has been said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber). The egg industry is just like every industry since the government came into power-it is sliding through to ruination. I could name the industries adversely affected if you wished, but you know them all. I know many people who ventured into the poultry business, and this year they are having a very hard time and not even meeting the cost of production from the sale of their eggs. I would not wait a day to apply the anti-dumping clause. An embargo should be put on the importation of eggs-not to-moiTow, but to-day. Give the Americans a dose of the medicine they gave us a few years ago, when after they had got all of our potatoes that they required they put an embargo on further importations and stuck us with hundreds of carloads of potatoes in transit to the border. I repeat, let us give them a bit of their own medicine and stop their eggs even in transit. This would not be any more unfair to them than the way they have used us in the past.

Did those

Here, Mr. Speaker, we

speechtext:
In the opinion of a very great number of people, who do not live at Weyburn, they certainly did. A half-hearted attempt was made by the government, in 1927, to deal with this question. Following the lead given by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stevens) when the Conservatives were in power for those few months, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler)) of this government issued an appraiser's bulletin in the end of January, 1927, providing for the current value for duty on eggs. That was followed, some few months later, by the current value for frozen eggs being also proclaimed. That had a most beneficial effect on the egg industry in Canada. Hope once more was raised and increased production took place, for this is one of those industries, a part of the great agricultural industry, in which it has been demonstrated over and over again that Canada is second to none in production, in quality, and that this industry can be fostered with reasonable assistance. The government, in 1928, saw fit for reasons, which they have proclaimed, to remove that which they had given, under their own minister, in January, 1927, and although those reasons may be sufficient to the government they have never appeared to be sufficient to those concerned in the egg industry in Canada, because we have the testimony of the chief of the poultry division, that the protection given on that occasion on Canadian eggs did not raise the price to the consumer. I quote from a memorandum prepared by that gentleman in April, 1927, as follows:
The invoking of the dumping duty has in no vra,v affected the Canadian consumer, who was required to pay no more for his eggs than heretofore. The retail prices of eggs following the invoking of the duty were, in fact, in many instances lower than the average of the past three years. On the other hand, the duty has been of the utmost advantage to producers in that it has wiped out many of the violent market fluctuations caused by seasonal and other conditions and has given them a steady, satisfactory and remunerative outlet for their nro-duct in 1927.
The egg industry had a taste, for a short time, of what reasonable assistance to their industry would produce, and it was with a great falling of heart that the producers noticed the government had removed that assistance. Since then the government has not seen fit to give them assistance. It seems to

me that because of its effect on the whole agricultural industry of this country it is a matter of most serious importance.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am heartily in accord with the motion brought down by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber). I think it is apparent to every person in this country that a grave injustice is being done to the poultry industry in Canada. As the member for Fraser Valley has said, the imports for January, 1929, amounted to 12,063 dozen. In January, 1930, they amounted to 536,848 dozen; for February, 1929, 74,730 dozen, and for February, 1930, 1,448,220 dozen. The total imports for the whole of the year 1929 amounted to 713,290 dozen. In other words, there were practically twice as many eggs imported in the month of February this year as there were for the whole of the year 1929. The duty, as we are aware, is 3 cents a dozen on eggs coming from the United States into Canada, and 8 cents a dozen on Canadian eggs going into the United States. If we take the difference between 3 cents and 8 cents, and take the imports for the month of February of this year, it amounts to approximately $75,000. Why should the Canadian poultry producer be under such a handicap? I do not want to quote figures at this time, Mr. Speaker, because the member for Fraser Valley has already quoted them. The member for Halt-on (Mr. Anderson) has said that the egg production of Canada is the highest per capita of any country in the world. In the year 1927 it was 29.20 dozen per hen.
The point I want to make is this, Mr. Speaker, that if the Canadian producer of eggs can supply eggs of such a quality that practically every man, woman and child in this country eats one egg a day, why should we not be sending those eggs to other countries? We should not be importing any eggs at all, but rather should we be exporting them. As one of the members for Toronto has said, if I had my way I would prohibit, or put an embargo on eggs coming in at all. Why do we not protect such an industry in every possible way?
I am very much in accord with this resolution, and I really believe the Prime Minister, since he is to a certain extent in the poultry business himself, should take this matter to heart and see that the other poor poultrymen get some protection.

More eggs are put on the market and the price begins to decline. A dealer will buy eggs today at, we will say, 50 cents per dozen. He finds that to-morrow the production is greater but he tries to hold up the price so that he can make profit on the eggs he bought yesterday. He does not lower the price, and what is the result? In 1913, under the Borden government, the importation of eggs into Canada amounted to 13,000,000 dozens at an average price of 21 cents per dozen. I do not think there was one word of complaint made at that time by the Tory party, then in office. In 1921, under the famous Union government, the importation of eggs amounted to 9,637,000 dozen at an average price of 30 cents per dozen, and still as far as I can find there was not a cackle out of the Tory party. Then the Liberals came into office and put into effect a system of egg grading. The quality improved, the consumption increased, and in 1928, strange as it may' seem, even under a Liberal government, importation of eggs dropped to approximately 1,000,000 dozen at an average price of 471 cents per dozen. During the same y'ear we exported about 500,000 dozen of eggs, so the net importation during that year amounted to about 500,000 dozen. Let us figure that upon the basis of consumption. We consume in Canada approximately 275,000,000 dozens of eggs annually, so figured upon that basis one egg in 550 was an imported egg. If considered upon the basis of the entire population of Canada, only one-half egg per capita per year was imported. Is it not a terrible thing to think that a great national party has to resort to tactics of this kind in order to obtain some publicity for themselves The Canadian hen controls 99-S per cent of the market, and if any newspaper controlled that percentage of the circulation in any one city it would feel that it ruled the roost. In this particular case the Canadian hen does rule the roost. Just think, if the Canadian hen laid one egg more in eight years, then she would supply the entire Canadian market. That she does not do that is the complaint which comes from across the floor of the house.
Let us come down to the year 1929. There has been a favourable progression in the egg business under the Liberal government. In the fiscal year ending March, 1929, we imported 1,128,000 dozens of eggs, and we exported 919.000 dozens, a net importation of only 209,000 dozens. We imported only one egg in 1,256 eggs consumed, and our Conservative friends ask us to stand like Horatius at the bridge defending this country from the onslaught of one egg in 1,256 consumed. The small areas we have in our farms are not adapted for anything but egg producing, and our iproducens go in for large numbers of birds. A flock of 10,000 birds is not unknown, and a flock of 3,000 or 4,000 is quite common.
I am in general accord with what I hope is the underlying motive that actuated hon. members from British Columbia in bringing up this matter, that is, if their motive is to bring pressure upon the government to afford some relief to the poultry business in British Columbia. I am not in sympathy with the manifold exaggerations and the patent political aspect which was sought to be given to this motion. The hon. member who introduced the resolution said, in the course of his remarks, that the egg industry had been given a stimulus. by the egg grading system that had been introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) a number of years ago. I have on my desk if I could put my hand on it, notice of a resolution introduced a few years ago by one of his colleagues, and largely supported by his side of the house, really a want of confidence motion, asking that the whole grading system be done away with. Now
I am glad to find him admitting that grading has been a good thing for the egg business and has resulted in enormously increasing consumption per head of population, and general production in Canada. I need not go into the figures. They show that the industry has increased enormously in spite of the handicaps which have been mentioned in course of the debate. I think it was the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) who was pleased to state that he saw some members on this side of the house smiling when the motion was introduced and he interpreted that as meaning that hon. members opposite to him regarded the matter as one of amusement and of no importance. I do not think it is within the scope of any hon. member to decide for the house what a man means when he smiles. A man when he smiles may be actuated by many motives. I think it was Shakespeare who said:
That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain.
But the *converse is true, that he may smile and smile and not be a villain. I had occasion to smile in connection with this matter, but it was not at the seriousness of the egg industry. It was because I heard the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) state that we ought to consume everything we grow in Canada, a sentiment which was applauded by my hon. friends opposite. Would it not make a cat smile to think of our eating all the wheat we grow in Canada?
What had a good deal to do with the conditions complained of by the mover of the motion was, as he or some other hon. member suggested, the withdrawal of the anti-dumping clauses imposed by the government a year or two ago. There is no doubt those clauses were working very satisfactorily and they heavily reduced the importation of United States eggs. With my hon. friends I share in regretting and deploring that the antidumping clauses were withdrawn. They have been in part compensated for, as I am able to admit, although my hon. friends opposite are not, by the imposition of a valuation of what are called frozen eggs, which valuation was very acceptable to the egg interests because it was the cause of largely, if not almost totally, keeping out the low grade eggs. Those are broken, cracked, dirty eggs that are frozen in the tins and sold by the pound. Owing to the fact that they were sold in that way and not subject to a specific duty, but to an ad valorem duty, it was possible for the Minister of Agriculture to do as he did, and place a fixed value on them, which I think was 45 cents, which made a

Let those who were privy to it defend it if they can. When he returned I called his attention to the matter and the valuation was promptly restored and it is still in effect. To show that I am sincere in this matter, I have under my hand the record of a vote which was taken on May 16, 1928, in which I was one of those who voted against the government on a want of confidence resolution on this same subject introduced by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson). I see that the vote was 59 to 110.
There are two remedies that I would suggest in connection with this matter: one is the very obvious one of increasing the duty, but I suggest that it would be sufficient, and would be justice to the consumer and producer alike, if this were imposed in a seasonal manner. I do not think the egg producers themselves demand that it be an all the year round duty, for fear that it would make the price of local eggs so high as to reduce the consumption, because it is a well known fact that consumption and price are closely related to each other. Again, I do not think the egg producers ask that the duty be increased on all classes of eggs. All they ask is that a tariff should be imposed on two specific grades. Therefore a seasonal duty will meet the situation and do justice to both sides of the argument, because there are two sides, the producer's and the consumer's.
[Mr. Neffl.1
Another suggestion that would have been of great benefit if it had been carried out was to introduce a measure making the British Columbia Egg Marking Act apply all over Canada. The house will remember that some years ago I introduced a resolution to that effect and the government, with some stipulation that, for some reason which they gave, it was not to be put into force for the moment, agreed to that. It passed the house.
I have made one or two attempts since then to ascertain why steps have not been taken to carry it out, and I have been told at least on one occasion very plainly by officers of the department that the people of British Columbia themselves no longer wish it; that they thought it would not be advisable for some reason. They thought it would be only an advertisement for the foreign eggs, and an instance in Great Britain was given where they passed a law that eggs should be marked with the country of origin. I think it was Danish eggs which they insisted on being marked, and it was discovered that instead of this being a deterrent to eggs coming in, it was a source of advertisement, because the eggs were put up in beautiful packages, well graded and consequently people who liked a good egg went back and asked for Danish eggs or whatever they were, instead of local eggs. Be that as it may, I do think that the act has been a success in British Columbia and that it might well be applied throughout the whole of Canada. It might be held that it would only have a sentimental value, but there is a good deal of sentiment in us all, and I think that a man sitting down to breakfast would be apt to say, "Why these foreign eggs? Why not Canadian eggs?" Therefore, I would suggest both a seasonal duty and the application of the British Columbia Egg Marking Act to the whole of Canada.

Mr. MeLEAN:	She was worth a whole

If I heard correctly, some statements have been made in this debate to the effect that last year our exports of eggs exceeded) our imports. In that connection I would say that after the various orders in council had been cancelled in 1928, during that year, when the order in council was abolished for the major portion of the year, our imports had been reduced from over 3,000,000 dozen eggs, worth $1,500,000. to less than 1,000,000 dozen, worth $425,000, or a reduction of nearly 70 per cent. At the same time, our exports of eggs increased from 448,000 dozen, worth $168,000, to 998,000 dozen, worth S346.000, or nearly 100 per cent. In 1927, our imports of eggs into Canada were more than seven times the volume of our exports, while in 1928, our imports and exports were at a virtual parity. If the effect of having restrictive orders in council was that we imported seven times as much in 1927 as we exported, and the abolition of the orders in council resulted in our exporting practically as much as we imported, I think it was a good thing to do away with these restrictive regulations.	_
Another argument has been made in support of the urgency of this motion, and that was in connection with the Canadian egg pool. I remember reading in the press a statement such as that which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) made. I do not mind saying that I agree with him, that in the opinion of the pool at that time Canadian production was not sufficient to take care of the market requirements, as was indicated a little while before that when eggs were coming in from Chicago and elsewhere, as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) has said, in response to telegraphic requests.
Many previous speakers have emphasized the fact that our increased importations were high in 1930 during the months of January, February and the beginning of March. There was a good reason for that. Surely hon. gentlemen know that the winter of 1929-30 has been

658	COMMONS
Importation of Eggs-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
one of the hardest winters Canada has experienced in possibly twenty-five years. During that hard weather winter, the hens of British Columbia were not very well prepared to meet such climatic conditions, and naturally one would expect a drop in production. I understand from visitors to that province that the winter there was very much more severe than usual, and consequently any advantage which that province has in the way of climate in an ordinary year was largely done away with. Other provinces being in the position of having to prepare for hard winters, usually are ready for them, and they were not so much affected. We are asked to adopt as a remedy for this state of affairs which came about as a result of the extremely cold weather, the remedy which has been adopted in the United States, and that is to increase the duty from 3 to 8 cents per dozen. It is just possible that similar causes would have similar effects, and if increasing the duty from 3 to 8 cents would have the effect on the poultry business in Canada that it apparently has had in the United States, I am entirely against it. We find in that country of high protection prices were suf-ciently low that they were able to send into this country all the eggs we wanted at a lower price than that which was being charged for Canadian produced eggs.
Something was said about high priced eggs for the sick room and it caused amusement among my hon. friends opposite. But they overlook the fact that the cheaper eggs coming into Montreal and Toronto-and apparently this is what gives rise to the complaint-help to supply many people with a wholesome food which they could not purchase were it at higher prices. I know a good many people throughout Canada to-day make their living from eggs, butter and other produce. If that is so, while it might suit the consumer to have the duty raised, if it would have the ultimate effect that it has produced in the United States, I do not think it would suit my hon. friends opposite, who are asking for an increase of duty in order to raise prices and shut off the influx of eggs from other countries.
My hon. friend from Toronto complained there would be no sense in going to the tariff board because the tariff board was the graveyard of Canadian industry. I think he would be the first to admit that he was exaggerating.

I hold in my hand an extract from the Manitoba Free Press of May 16, 1929, in which it is said:
The increase asked in the application is from 3 cents to 9 cents on every dozen of eggs brought into Canada in the "extras" class. . .
The hearing was adjourned at the request of the applicants until some date in July or August, to be decided later.
The hearing has been delayed from time to time ever since, and it is very doubtful if the application will be proceeded with.
There was one other matter that, I must say, surprised me in the claim of my hon. friends opposite. I remember four years ago-just before an election I might say-that the attention of this house was called by an hon. member from British Columbia to the condition of the poultry industry in his province. He said it was just about on its last legs and ready to give up the ghost. Apparently it revived in the meantime and became very prosperous, because the value of our egg production has increased from $40,000,000 to $84,000,000 per annum, and a large part of this increase must be due to the egg producers of British Columbia. Now that industry, they say, is in a very bad way. During the debate on that occasion I suggested that there were other causes for the difficulties of the British Columbia egg producers besides any lack of duty, but I did not find much support for my viewpoint from hon. members opposite. I am going to suggest to them that apparently they are on the wrong track entirety in urging that lack of duty is the whole trouble. In fact one hon. member to-day said that lack of tariff protection was the entire cause of the importation of eggs from the United States, and this importation accounted for the failure of the men on the land out in British Columbia. In the same copy of the Manitoba Free Press, in a parallel column on the same page,
I find these headlines:
B.C. Farmers Appeal to Prairie Brethren.
Poultry raisers declare prices of feed driving them out of business.
Grievance aired before Saskatchewan grain commission at Vancouver.
I have read the despatch and I do not find in it one word of complaint from the tariff standpoint. Let me quote two or three paragraphs:
A cry for help addressed to the farmers of Saskatchewan and Alberta has come from

those engaged in agricultural production in British Columbia. The Saskatchewan grain commission to-day devoted its sitting hours to hearing troubles and tribulations of British Columbia agriculturists, especially as concerns poultry raisers who are dependent upon feed grains from producers of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
"Unless something is done to enable us to get our feed grains from the producers of Saskatchewan and Alberta at a reasonable rate, poultry raisers of the Fraser river valley and other parts will be compelled to go out of business." This is the way their problem was put by half a dozen farmers who were piloted through their stories by G. G. McGeer, K.C., legal advisor to B. C. organized farmers.
Freight rates encircle the whole question, and, according to one witness, threaten to strangle the poultry producer here and close a profitable market for feed grain of the Saskatchewan farmer.
I would dea-l for a moment with the remark made by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), I think it was, who spoke about soldier settlement. Here is a farmer giving evidence .before the Saskatchewan grain commission, and this is another paragraph in the despatch from which I have already quoted:
Special despatch to the Free Press
Vancouver B.C., May 15.
How a Saskatchewan farmer sold his holdings, located near Shaunavon, and, five months ago. packed his family and goods and moved to Sunny, B.C., to engage in chicken raising, and in this period finds that he is now several hundred dollars on the wrong side of the ledger, was unfolded to the commission to-day. He is M. H. Swanson, and from 1913 to 1928 farmed 25 miles south of Shaunavon. "I made a big mistake when I came here from the prairies to engage in chicken farming," he said "and I want to get back to Saskatchewan."
Here again a contributing important factor to his failure is cited as the high cost of feed. He pays $2.20 per 100 pounds for low feed from Saskatchewan, for which, when he farmed, he received 35 to 50 cents a bushel.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that British Columbia has not all the advantages in poultry production that are sometimes claimed for that province, and if egg producers embark on the poultry business in British Columbia on account of the climatic advantages, they surely must figure beforehand on the cost of feed, the cost of freight, the difficulties that they will have in getting their products to other markets in Canada, and the competition they will be up against from other centres whose people producing eggs have more real advantages than obtain where the winters are mild.
A learned American professor was quoted in this house the other day by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-
2419-42J
Professor Taussig. Naturally I suppose it is open to anyone to quote the same authority. Professor Taussig points out this fact, that American inventive genius and American technical skill were infinitely greater factors in American prosperity than the protective tariff. It is so also with the Canadian poultry industry. The Canadian poultry industry owes its success to the great work of the poultry breeders, the cooperative marketing associations, the assistance given by the government in encouraging such work as grading, the extension of markets, and in other ways. Science, technical skill, inventive genius, efficient marketing-these are the basic causes of the success of our poultry industry.

I repeat what I said, that the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, as I heard them-and I followed him very closely-seemed to me to be chiefly a ridiculing of those engaged in the poultry industry in British Columbia. One of the observations he made was this: he referred to the champion egg-laying hen in Saskatchewan-and by the way, I think it was a most excellent performance; I mean the hen's performance, not my hon. friend's. It is a most encouraging thing to the poultry industry of Canada that this particular hen to which he refers, and others as well, should under special circumstances have made such records, and I have no doubt at all that it has largely contributed to the increased production of eggs, and also to the improvement of the industry. But, my hon. friend said, if the poultry industry in British Columbia, which had increased its average only from 78 to 95 a year, would take a pattern from this particular Saskatchewan hen, then the poultry-men in British Columbia would not have so much complaint. My hon. friend was quoting from the official record of the average production per hen for the whole of Canada, which I have in my hand, page 118, showing

that in 1921 it was 78 and in 1928 it had risen to 95. That is the average for the whole of Canada and not for British Columbia. I merely cite that as an evidence of the unfairness of the references.
Now, my hon. friends opposite seem not to like very well the observations made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house, so I am going to read from an editorial taken from the Vancouver Sun, the outstanding Liberal paper in British Columbia. The editorial has this to say on the subject-and I commend it to the attention of the government and of hon. gentlemen supporting the government who are se very eloquently ridiculing this proposal today:
It costs 8 cents in duty to ship a dozen Canadian eggs into the United States. It costs 3 cents in duty to ship a dozen American eggs into Canada. This means that the Canadian market can be flooded with American eggs at any time such flooding is convenient to the American producer while the Canadian eggs are practically shut out of the American market at all seasons of the year.
I pause now in order to emphasize this very point. The editor of this paper is making the vary argument that, we are trying to impress upon the government at this time with regard to the condition brought about by the heavy duty against Canadian eggs, by which we are virtually shut out of the American market. When there is a large production of eggs in Canada they must all be absorbed in Canada, either by immediate consumption or by what is a very splendid thing, cold storage -sitting aside eggs for the period of the year when there is a lower production-While on the other hand at certain seasons of the year, and particularly in the more moderate climates in the United States, they can relieve the over-production by dumping the surplus into our market at a very low rate of duty. And the editor of the paper puts his finger on that particular fact, and calls attention to it. Then he goes on to aay:
The poultry industry of British Columbia has produced an egg that stands superior to the product of any other poultry district in the world. On the basis of quality it should command a premium in any market.
And I pause to say that I agree with my hon. friend from Melfort (Mr. McLean) that due to the activities of governments, provincial and Dominion, to the efforts of poultry-men, and to more scientific methods of production, we have raised the standard of eggs, and you can buy a much better product on the market to-day than you could a few years ago. You get larger and better eggs. No. 1

Importation oj Eggs-Mr. Stevens
grade egg is a splendid, superior article. These things have all contributed to that end, and we have built up an industry. The point we are trying to make is this: Why should that industry, at 'Certain seasons of the year, be subjected to such unfair competition that advantages gained by long and serious effort are largely destroyed?
The editorial goes on to say:
But what encouragement is there for British Columbia poultrymen to carry on their industry in a scientific and expert way when their quality product is crowded out of the markets by American eggs that are allowed in under an inadequate tariff?
That is the point. That is what this paper is asking, and that is the question we are putting to the government; we are endeavouring to direct attention to that important problem.
The editorial continues:
The obvious and natural arrangement between Canada and United States would be absolute free trade in eggs-a system that would allow both products to compete on their merits.
It is the editor of this Liberal paper who makes that statement. He goes on to say this:
Tariff has never been a national issue in Canada, But, so long as the United States maintains its tariff wall, Canadian poultrymen are entitled to the protection of a reciprocal tariff. And it should be one of the first jobs of the tariff board to give it to them.

That is the objective, and I think efforts such as those we have been referring to are largely contributing to the attainment of that objective.
The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) used an argument just now that really was not worthy of his scintillating intelligence. He narrowed the importation down to half an egg a day to the people of Canada. Now, what are the facts? We are talking about what is happening now, not what happened in 1921, 1922, or any other time. The fact is that in the months of January and February of this year the importations amounted to 1,600,000 dozen eggs. That is the fact; these eggs are invading our market to such an extent as to imperil the poultry industry of this country.

I am going to deal with
that very point shortly, if my non. friend will follow me. The poultry industry is something like ihe butter industry in Canada; it is more or less seasonal. In other words, at some seasons of the year you can produce butter much more cheaply than at others, and) the result over a long period of years has been that we have taken the surplus butter produced during the period of over-production, if you like, or the period of cheap production, and placed it in cold storage plants, largely developed at the expense of the government and the taxpayers of this country. This cold storage system enables us to store cheaply and safely butter and other perishable goods in order to carry over from the flood season into the sparse season some portion of the over-production, and thus more or less equalize prices and supply.
The same thing applies to poultry; by our system of cold storage-and again I point out that it was developed at great public expense -we are enabled to carry eggs over to that period of the year when poultry do not produce so freely. It does mot matter very much what may be the habits of the hens; the point is that nature has provided that at certain seasons poultry will moult and will not lay eggs, and in this climate, when it is exceedingly cold production will naturally fall off. On the other hand, there are certain seasons when the production rises very rapidly; that is noticeable in the spring of the year, during the months of March, April, May and so on, and if we are to develop this industry in these months, production necessarily and naturally must out-rum consumption.

Importation of Eggs-Mr. Stevens
Whether you deal with money as such, with manufactured products, or more particularly with farm products, the great problem before all students of economy is how to stabilize production. The question, is how to conserve production to a point where it can be fed out at a rate which will be equitable and suitable to the consuming demand. That is a great problem. We have solved it in large measure in this particular branch of agriculture, in, other words in dairying and1,poultry.
Let us consider the question of poultry for table use. Poultry for table consumption is in great demand around the Christmas season, but of course the practice has been to kill the 'poultry at the most suitable time of the year, put it in cold storage, and then feed it. out to the market when the demand is greater1. In that way the producer undoubtedly gets an advantage, to which he is entitled. My hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) emphasizes constantly in this house the right of the consumer, but in all his arguments he is constantly losing sight of the right of the producer. If I were asked to choose between the man who is producing from the soil, whether it be wheat or poultry or anything in that nature, and the consumer as such, I would choose to support the interests of the producer.

In regard to that question we must enter into a discussion of the culinary use of eggs. For ordinary cooking purposes, and in a very large measure for eating, the cold storage egg which has been properly selected, graded and stored soon after it has been produced is almost as good as the fresh egg. If the most uip-to-date storage methods are used, that egg is almost as good as a strictly fresh egg. My hon. friend asks which I would prefer. Unquestionably I would prefer the strictly new-laid egg; there is no doubt about that, but I say that for culinary purposes and for ordinary market use the cold storage egg which is properly handled, stored and looked after, is almost as good as the fresh egg. I will say further, tlhat through the efforts of this government-and by that I mean -the federal government for the last twenty years-and the efforts of provincial governments, the system of cold storage has been so completely changed and so greatly improved that cold storage to-day is one of the best servants of the public.
My hon. friend referred a moment ago to the difficulties of the producer in British Columbia owing to the cost of feed. The question there is one which demands very close attention. The consumer of feed wheat on the Pacific coast, we will say, must pay double the freight rate which is paid on export wheat. I will give the figures roughly from memory; 1 think the rate on export wheat is 20 cents per hundred, while the rate on feed wheat is 41i cents per hundred. In other words, the man who buys a hundred pounds of wheat feed for his chickens has to pay a freight rate which is more than double the rate applicable to export wheat, and in addition he buys a cheaper grade of wheat, a wheat which perhaps is little off grade but good enough for feed. Therefore the rate of 41i cents per hundred constitutes a very substantial portion of the cost of that wheat. That is the thing about which we are complaining, and the man who goes into the poultry business finds it a very serious matter. He starts out with perhaps two or three acres of land; he has an expensive plant requiring quite a large capital investment; he puts up sanitary, modern buildings; he buys his feed; he keeps

special scratch and all the rest of it; he watches his poultry and keeps them healthy; he gathers his eggs; he markets them extremely fresh, by the pool system; and with all this expense and ail this effort he finds himself faced with exorbitant freight rates. That is the ground of their complaint, and it is not an unfair one.

reason. Suppose a carload of feed is shipped to Vancouver which must be distributed, by truck and at considerable expense, over a large area where the poultry farms are located. Take Vancouver island, for instance. A carload of wheat will be landed at Victoria and from there it must go up the island probably two hundred or more miles and be distributed at a dozen points, a few sacks here and a few sacks there. Naturally that adds to the cost, but the major complaint is against the excessive freight rates. But that does not affect the seriousness of the problem which we are bringing to the attention of parliament and of the country, namely, the sudden, unexpected, irregular and more or less hazardous importation of eggs during certain seasons of the year. If the consuming market in the United States happens to be in a buoyant condition, if the overseas market is attractive, our American friends at once divert their surplus in those directions, but should it happen that during January and February, which is spring in the warmer states, they are faced with an oversupply and the local market seems to be getting a little flat, they ship a dozen cars into Toronto or Montreal, thus solving their problem in Chicago, New York, Cincinatti and other places. They are able to maintain their own price and incidentally break our market.
I think the appeal of the poultry pools of British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and other sections of Canada is one which merits consideration and ought to have the thoughtful attention of the government. If we can in any way, by action of this parliament or of the government, stabilize the egg market and give to the poultry industry reasonable assistance in relieving it of this sudden, unexpected and unfair competition, then I think it is only the right and proper thing to do.

I quite agree with that, but my hon. friend will admit- that our problem in Canada has been to dispose of our low grade eggs. When the duty value on bulk eggs was made higher a market was made for the lower grade of eggs. That was very helpful, and the whole question should be considered together.
Returning to the question of cold storage: I have before me the record of eggs in cold storage for the 'period 1925 to 1930. In February, 1928, we had in storage about 1,000,000 dozens of eggs, while in January of that year we had in storage 2,500,000 dozens. The eggs in storage seem to reach their peak between June and October, the peak ranging from
12,000,000 to 16,000,000 dozens. In September 1927 we had 15,000,000 dozens of eggs in storage, and by February, 192S, the amount had decreased to 1,250,000 dozens, while it had been 2,500,000 dozens in January.
Compare conditions as they existed in January and February of 1929, with the conditions existing in January and February of 1930. In September, 1929, we had in store ' 15,000,000 dozens eggs, by January of this year that figure had decreased to 862,000 dozens and by February it had decreased to practically 200,000 dozens. In other words, in February we came nearer to the point of depletion of eggs in storage than at any period since we started cold storage.
I contend that there is nothing abnormal in this heavy importation. With our production increasing, I do not see how this importation can continue. The importation came at a time when the eggs in store were depleted. At the same time there was a heavy demand for eggs, and, due to certain climatic conditions in British Columbia which have been referred to, the production from that province dropped very materially during December and January.
Other hon. members have made many statements, but let me say this in a general way: There is no question that the poultry industry, in so far as its returns from egg production are concerned, has in the past seven years had a most phenomenal growth. An industry that has grown from $40,000,000 to $84,000,000 in seven years has much to be said to its credit. It is also true, as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Garland) said, that we have reached, in the raising of poultry, a place which is second to none in

the world, and we have undoubtedly helped egg production by our grading system. I recall the speech of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) when he said that the farmers of his district were being injured to an enormous extent by this regulation which the Minister of Agriculture had iput into effect, but in spite of all that was said against egg grading, we find to-day unanimity in the house on this method of handling eggs. This industry has unquestionably prospered to a marked extent when it has more than doubled in the short space of seven years.

I was not aware of it. Egg -producers' associations have not petitioned the government on the question of egg importations. I believe my hon. friends opposite are ahead of the associations in making their plea to the government.
I want, however, to discuss one or two matters. The consumption of eggs in this country is practically 300,000,000 dozens, while the production is practically the same. The amount of variation between our production and consumption is so infinitesimally small' that it resolves itself into a part of one per cent. In 1928 our total importation of eggs, even putting it at 3,000,000, which includes in dozens all the eggs we imported in cans, was only one per cent of our total production or total consumption, whichever way >ou like to put it. Taking off the importation list the eggs which we import in cans, we had in 1929 a very much smaller importation in eggs and a substantial export at the same time. But hon. gentlemen opposite say that we ought to be in the egg export business; that we ought to foe exporting eggs in great quantities. Hon. gentlemen at the same time argue that we cannot produce eggs profitably at 45 cents per dozen, and they also know that eggs are higher in Canada to-day than they are in the United States or Great Britain. How are you going to go into the export business if you cannot make money at home prices which are higher than export prices? You cannot have it 'both ways. I have argued insistently in the house as to the value of the home market; I have been an advocate of it. It is quite true that our home market price to-day is substantially higher than the price in the United States.

Any figures I have given have been hurriedly secured. The argument advanced in regard to cold storage eggs was that in the years of which we have a record, there was no case in February where the quantity of eggs in storage had so nearly reached the depletion point as this year, and if there was any justification for the importation of eggs, it was due to the egg situation. There had been a decrease in production, as hon. gentlemen have pointed
out-I cannot give the figures-but it was said that in December and January weather conditions in British Columbia were so severe that production was smaller. If production was smaller in British Columbia in January and February and if the amount of eggs in storage had reached the vanishing point, it was only to be expected that the market would have to be supplied at that particular time by importation. Therefore, if the importation of eggs was greater in January and February whereas in other years it was greater in March, that was not to be wondered at. The low point for storage eggs in 1927, 1928, and 1929 has come in March. In January of each of these years there has been about one million dozen in storage, but in March it has always dropped down to about 250,000. This year, strangely enough, the low point of storage eggs was reached in Januajy and February, and instead of there being 2,500.000 dozens in store in January, as in 1929, there were only 682,000. And instead of 1.000,000 dozen in February, there were only 220,000.

speechtext:
I do not think it is a
great importation. I am trying to show my hon. friend that until the end of 1930 you cannot take any figures for the year with respect to production or export or import. My hon. friend is contending that there is an alarming situation because in a month where we generally do not have a heavy importation, heavy importation has occurred. I am showing that there was a direct reason for that heavy importation coming in February rather than in March, because it has been shown by hon. members who spoke that in other years the bulk of our production usually came in the month of March. It is not sufficiently heavy to be referred to as bulk; we are using a very extravagant expression so far as imports are concerned, because they comprise such a small part of our total production at any time. My hon. friend probably wants to argue that the poultry industry, like the dairy industry and other similar industries, can be bolstered up by the imposition of higher duties. Is that his point? Is that the point of hon. gentlemen opposite? Let us be perfectly frank. Hon. gentlemen opposite say:	Yes,
we can increase the production of butter and eggs in Canada by bolstering the price. All right; let us do that. But I want the farmers of Canada to realize that they have to choose between a mighty low world market price today on both butter and eggs, and the home market price, and the minute you put a high, enough duty on eggs you will get exactly the same condition which they have in the United States, over-production with very low prices

based on world prices. The minute you put a high duty on butter you will get exactly the same condition that obtains in other countries to-day. If Canada were on an export basis for butter, which my hon. friends opposite say is desirable, Canada's butter producers would be taking world prices.
I have never been a low tariff man, as everyone knows; I have never been a high tariff man. Every tariff item has to be considered on its own merits. It is an economic problem that has to be considered with relation to the conditions in other countries. But I will say this to my hon. friends, that the minute you get a tariff past the point where it is advisable, you stimulate internal competition, which is worse than outside competition. There are industries by the score in the United States to-day that are suffering from an excess of internal competition. I think the poultry industry furnishes very good evidence of that, in the prices ruling for eggs in the United States. You must analyse the poultry industry as a whole.
It has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I repeat this because I think the argument is worthy of consideration, and it has been implied by others in the questions which they have asked, that the poultry industry is not making money with eggs at 40 or 45 cents a dozen. If the poultry industry cannot survive at that price, it certainly cannot survive at world prices. It cannot survive at the price which is being obtained in the United States or in England, even if the tariff barriers were taken down entirely. If the poultry industry was made to increase its volume one per cent, it would be beyound the point of consumption in Canada, and that one per cent would have to be exported and would be a factor in regulating the price of eggs in Canada. My opinion is that purely as an economic argument-and I have argued this with poultry producers very many of whom I number amongst my friends-that at present in Canada the poultry producers are at as near a balance as they can ever hope to be. They are receiving a higher price than the world price. They control ninety-nine per cent of their own market, and any change in fiscal policy affecting the poultry industry would in my opinion do one of two things: To lower the duty would hurt the industry, because a greater importation of American eggs would tend to bring our price nearer to the American Price, which is below ours. To raise the duty would increase production, but that would put prices nearer to an export basis. I am not sufficiently acquainted with the economics of the poultry industry, and especially of the

Importation of Eggs-Mr. Rowe
egg industry, to say that 21 or 3 or 4 cents would be exactly the rate of duty to impose upon American eggs, but I do know this, that the representatives of the poultry producers went to the tariff board. The government, and especially the Minister of Finance, was anxious that they should present their case before that board. The government was willing to listen to the recommendations of the tariff board after they had heard the representatives of the poultry producers, but the poultry producers have never gone on with their case. They have never submitted the facts. They have asked for adjournment after adjournment. This is now, I believe, the fourth adjournment they have requested.
Will hon. gentlemen look at these facts? Here is an industry that has doubled production in seven years, an industry that has ninety-nine per cent of its home market, an industry that practically exports as much as it imports, an industry that has during this particular year, due to peculiar conditions, to import eggs one month earlier than in previous years because of a shortage in storage, an industry that has asked for an adjournment four times in the presentation of its case to the tariff board, and we are now asked that this industry should receive special consideration and that the house be adjourned to deal with it because its situation constitutes a great national calamity.

Well, I ask, is that tariff
added to the price that the domestic consumer has to pay for furniture; or is the tariff imposed in order that our furniture manufacturers may enjoy world wide trade? I ask if this great basic industry of agriculture is to be maintained on a sound economic basis by trying to keep the domestic supply in proper relation to consumption? The uncertainty of consumption has been pointed out. The Minister of Agriculture has told us that we have been eating too much butter. I think he told us that the Tory party are going to try to slide into power on butter. The consumption of eggs is uncertain, and I submit that consumption is a great deal more uncertain when you place on eggs a tariff of only 3 cents a dozen, which is equivalent to only 10 per cent at the present low price. Of course, this encourages importation. We need not worry how many eggs come in in one month or another month; the truth of the situation is that the uncertainty of the importation is what makes our home market uncertain. We know that full well.
So far we have not had many members on the other side of the house from Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba taking part in this debate. I see many of my friends on the other side who may ask:	"What business
have you to speak for our provinces?" Perhaps not very much, but I know a lot of Cotn-

servatives out there are waiting for an opportunity to speak on this question. But I am directing attention to the western provinces in order to bring before the house a letter written in reply to an article which appeared not so very long ago in the Ottawa Citizen from the pen of Mr. Deachman, the champion of western free trade ideas, in fact the man who sometimes has apparently more influence on the government than some of its own supporters in this house. Mr. Deachman had written an article entitled The Duty on Eggs, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of April 7, 1929. To this article M. W. A. Landreth, president and superintendent of the Canadian Poultry Pool, Limited, Winnipeg, replied in a 'letter which was published in the same paper on May 15, 1929, as follows:
We feel assured that the readers of your publication will be interested in the statistical information which it contains. May we point out, however, that statistics are a dangerous weapon in the hands of some one who may not be familiar with the industry which he endeavours to portray. Mr. Deachman has very ably pointed out the fact that Canadian poultry producers are now in a position to supply Canadian consumption of eggs. He has stated that all imports were made at a time when eggs were 47.6 cents per dozen wholesale. At this point. Mr. Deachman ceases to be an authority. His theories are exploded, and he must be classed with the uninformed.
True, large importations arrived on the Canadian markets when the wholesale price for Canadian eggs averaged over 40 cents per dozen, but due to importation of American eggs, many of which came in on consignment to be sold to the highest bidder, our Canadian market slumped. American eggs were offered on the Toronto market well under 30 cents per dozen, and holders of Canadian eggs were obliged to sell as low as 23 cents per dozen, f.o.b. Montreal.
The poultry producers of western Canada-
The poultry producers, mark you. I want to draw the attention of the bon. members for Melfort (Mr. McLean) and Weyburn (Mr. Young) to this fact:
The poultry producers of western Canada are not requesting protection for the purpose of inflating the price of eggs to the consumer. They desire protection because they believe that the best interests of the producer and the consumer can only be protected by a stabilized market. They wish to protect the distributors who purchase large quantities during the period of over-production, and who place them in store in order to protect the consumer from over inflation during the period of low production. We are sure your readers will agree, that if importation of less than one per cent of our production wrecked our Canadian market last season to the extent that many large distributors are afraid to buy for storage this season, in fairness to a growing Canadian industry, we should be protected against a recurrence in 1929.

Importation of Eggs-Mr. Rowe
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think that is a very reasonable statement, and it is true of what is happening all along the line. The uncertainty of the market for all lines of agricultural products is the greatest handicap of Canadian agriculture at the present time. We have been dealing with eggs, but in any other line of agricultural production a similar situation exists. Much has been said about eggs coming down to the Toronto market from British Columbia. I say to my bon. friends opposite that we on this side of the house are not concerned. We believe in interprovincial trade, and British Columbia eggs are welcome. They come in herein October, November and December, when our hens in Ontario are slowing down in egg production. We have been told about the increased egg production in the western provinces, and the hon. member for Melfort has referred to a hen raised by Professor Barker of the university ' of Saskatchewan which has broken the world's record for egg production. True, she was an exceptional hen. The former world's record was 314 eggs; last year the experimental farm here had a hen that laid 314 eggs; later British Columbia captured the record with, a hen that laid 351 eggs, and last year Professor Barker's hen laid 358 eggs.
