I doubt very much if we did. If the Minister of Finance will look up the records I think he will find that we were getting a much higher price in 1920 than we were last year. I submit that we were selling at. a higher price than we are this year because on Saturday last eggs were selling at 30 cents a dozen in Toronto. That, again, is due to the fluctuation of markets caused by the recent importations. How are we going to equalize agricultural industry with our manufacturing industries, as many have been talking up and down the side lines of this Dominion for years, unless this basic industry is adequately protected? We must redress the difficulties that now exist by equalizing conditions between these two great phases of our national life-agricultural and industry. How can the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn), the hon. member for Melfort
and the hon. member for Weyburn rise in their places and support a government that they know is giving protection ranging from 30 to 35 per cent to other industrial activities, and treat more or less as a joke the proposition we are bringing before this house? Why the hon. member for West Elgin referred to another resolution the other day in a more or less jocular spirit. There is no phase of agriculture in this country that serves as many people as the poultry and egg industry. Anyone who knows rural conditions knows full well-the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows full well-that the fanner who is in hard circumstances often pays his taxes and buys his wife's clothes out of the poultry, eggs and butter that he sells. They know, too, that the labouring man who works for the farmer, and who lives by the side of the road, with his children running around in their bare feet, probably keeps from twelve to twenty-five'hens, which is practically all that stands between them and starvation at times when he cannot secure work.
This is a very serious question, Mr. Speaker, for the people of this country. There is no other industry that is so little protected as the agricultural industry. Practically every man who works for the farmer has at least a few hens to look after, sometimes thirty, sometimes forty; in many years he makes as much $250 out of his hens, which goes a long way with what he gets for his whole year's work on the farm to keep his wife and family. As I say, Mr. Speaker, this matter is vitally important to the people of Canada, and at the next election this government will come to realize that the electors do regard it as important. Opinions are being expressed today all the way down the line, pointing to the fact that we have had no consideration. We were told a few years ago by hon. members representing western constituencies, and presumably representing western thought, to produce more. The government told the people a few years ago to produce more; in fact they searched from one end of the globe to the other to find markets for us. We on this side make the statement-acquiesced in to a great extent by those on the other side-that it is not fair to those who work in manufacturing establishments in this country to have to compete with the sweat shops of Europe and other places, and similarly it is not fair that our agriculturists should be asked to compete with those of European countries with their much lower standard condition of living. It it is high time that no matter what government assumes the reins of office agricultural products Should have a fairer measure of protection. I know, too, that the people of Melfort, West

Importation oj Eggs-Mr. Rowe
Elgin and Weyburn, when they read Hansard, and read it [DOT]carefully, will say to themselves: "Well, I do not think that it is such a joke as our representatives seem to think it is. Our very existence is at stake; our condition is ted; our return for the year has been much smaller than for other years, and agriculture generally has suffered more than it has done during the last twenty years. It is high time that we received from this government some consideration, or some unanimity of thought." Egg markets throughout Canada are in a very uncertain condition. Production everywhere has grown termendously during the past week and values have undergone some very drastic declines. Prices are now considerably lower than at the corresponding time for the past two years and are, in fact, already down to a storage basis at a number of points in the producing areas. This applies more chiefly to the four -western provinces. A great proportion of the blame for the present condition of the market may be traced directly to the rapid and extreme price declines on American markets and to the heavy importations which have been brought in from that country. Western markets, with a surplus over local requirements, are endeavouring to unload carloads in the east, but are finding markets in that section already well supplied with imported stocks. It is improbable that any further importations will be made during the present season but until these stocks which have already been brought in are cleaned up the outlet for surplus stocks in producing sections will probably be limited.
Montreal during recent weeks has been bringing in about fifteen cars of United States eggs weekly. With the sudden rush of local production, however, it would appear that imports during the past week have been a little heavier than were required. This, of course, is a very difficult factor to estimate and some overstocking is almost inevitable under such conditions. What the future holds for the coming spring egg season is very difficult to forecast. There are a number of factors to be taken into consideration. Undoubtedly the season is getting off to a poor start in so far as prices are concerned. Already values in the west are down to a storage basis, with some eggs actually moving into the coolers at the present time. Danger of chilled eggs, a very undesirable product for storing, is not yet past, but with stocks accumulating and no demand from the east, western operators are left with little alternative but to place the surplus in storage. In a sense it is not unfortunate that prices have declined rather rapidly. The storing of eggs at the present time will act as a deterrent against ally further declines and will give stocks on hand a chance to clear without being loaded up by further surplus. Once this is achieved a much healthier situation may be expected to develop. It should be borne in mind, also, that the present low prices for eggs are bound to result in a tremendous increase in consumption. This is a very important factor and will have a great deal of significance on the market during the next few weeks.
It is inevitable, of course, that the United States prices will continue to exert considerable influence on the trend of values in this country. It appears to be the general impression in the states that the coming spring will see a very heavy production but the same conditions which may be expected to bring about a reaction on Canadian markets are also being exerted in the United States and some upward trend from the present low levels W'ould not appear to be improbable.
At this time it is rather interesting to note the manner in which the present year has completely reversed the order of last year in so far as egg supplies and prices are concerned. The month of January this year saw a shortage of eggs. Last year in January there was a considerable surplus. Importations from the United States were exceptionally heavy during the present January and February. There were some importations last year during that time but at Montreal, for instance, the heavy imports of eggs did not get under way until about the 8th of March.

He-the mover-then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to he discussed to the Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house. If objection is taken, the Speaker requests those members who support the motion to rise in their places and if more than twenty members rise accordingly, the Speaker calls upon the member who has asked for leave.
What happened this afternoon? The motion was handed to the Speaker, who looked around; he had his doubts, I am sure, as to the urgency of this egg question, but twenty members rose, no one protested, and the debate went on. Under rule 31, Beauchesne states at paragraph 249:

In doubtful cases, the question of urgency and of importance are left for the house to decide by giving or withholding its support.
This afternoon that support was given to the presentation of the motion and therefore, under the circumstances, without committing the Chair for future motions of a similar nature, the debate must go on.
I hope hon. members will not travel too far afield and that they will concentrate on eggs. It is said that one cannot make an omelette without breaking eggs. This is a case in point, where one should refer to eggs only.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel very grateful indeed that you agree with members on this side of the house that this question is of great and urgent public importance, and I am sure that the constituents of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and of the hon. members for Weyburn (Mr. Young), Melfort (Mr. McLean), Lisgar (Mr. Brown), and other constituencies will be very much interested when they find that their respective members do not consider this matter to be of great public importance. This industry produces annually agricultural products to the value of nearly
8100.000,000, which amount would be considerably increased if we considered the value of poultry as well as of eggs, and anything that affects detrimentally this great industry immediately becomes a matter of urgent public importance.
The price of eggs to-day is lower than it has been in the corresponding months as far back as hon. members can remember. What has depressed the price of eggs at this particular time of the year? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) and other hon. members have said that the supply of eggs is not equal to the demand, and that this condition has brought about some importation, while the hon. members for Lisgar, Weyburn, Melfort and so on have said that the imports are infinitesimal when compared to the total production. I admit all that, but I contend that without the importation of one egg the price of eggs could be depressed. The price has been depressed from 50 cents to 30 cents per dozen, which depression could be brought about by one American quotation in the city of Toronto or the city of Montreal. When such a quotation is made the market price is automatically depressed to the price at which such eggs are offered. It is not a question of whether or not the supply of eggs coming from a foreign country is infinitesimal as compared to the total consumption or total production.

Importation oj Eggs-Mr. Clark
the whole test is whether there is a country with an available supply which can be offered at low prices. That is what has happened. Thi9 house has never heard hon. members form this side object to competition within Canada; the farmers represented by members on this side of the house do not object to legitimate competition from farmers within Canada, but whether we represent urban or rural constituencies we do object to unfair competition from foreign countries when our producers can be protected against such competition. British Volumbia eggs are being accumulated in Vancouver and are available at fair prices to the markets of eastern Canada, but this government has permitted the price of eggs to be depressed to a point where the producers of British Columbia cannot afford to send eggs to the eastern markets. We ask that the Canadian producer be given an opportunity to compete in the markets of Canada.
I was astounded at hearing the one member of the cabinet who rose in his place to defend the position of the government declaring for the policy of the Conservative party. He said that when a product is protected competition follows automatically and production increases. In that way we would have more Canadians producing our products, and not more Americans. We do not object to the price being depressed so long as it is depressed by fair competition within Canada. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has made the strongest argument which could be made for his department, namely, that when this industry or any other industry is given a fair amount of protection the production is increased within Canada and the price is automatically adjusted; supply and demand work automatically to produce a fair price for the commodity, and whether it be eggs or other products, they will have an opportunity of entering the world markets. WThat we are interested in knowing is whether or not the cabinet and the Liberal party agree with the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the only member of the cabinet who has spoken to-day. It is an extraordinary spectacle and one which should be drawn to the attention of the house, that the members of the cabinet have been conspicuous by their absence throughout the debate.
This matter should be of particular interest to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). I do not desire to criticize the absence of the minister if that absence is due to ill health, but surely there is an acting minister of agriculture who could express his
ideas as to what should be done for this great industry. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) should be interested in this subject, as it is his duty as much as the duty of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture to give an expression of the government's policy in this matter. We have heard nothing from the government except the Minister of Trade and Commerce who has laid down the doctrine of this party, which doctrine is flatly contradicted by the supporters of the government who have spoken.	,
The members of the house are interested in knowing whether or not we have a minister of trade and commerce for the United States and a minister of agriculture for the United States. Whether one examines the trade with the United States or the trade treaty with France or the trade treaty with Italy, the same result will be found. In 1920 we had a surplus of trade with France amounting to 850,000,000, but that has been changed to an adverse balance of 810,000,000. The balance of trade with Italy amounted to over $56,000,000 in 1921, and it has been reduced to about $7,000,000.
I regret to hear the hon. members across the floor of the house treat this matter as a joke, and I regret hearing the hon. Minister of Finance argue that this is not a matter of urgent public importance. As a representative of one of the great cities of Canada I think I represent the consumer, even more so than the hon. member for Weyburn and other hon. members of the Liberal party, and I believe that the people of Vancouver, as well as the people of the other great cities of Canada, are quite prepared to support the agricultural interests of this country. They are quite prepared to pay fair prices for agricultural products and are quite prepared to support that industry so that it may become and continue to be one of the prosperous industries of the country.

subtopic: CANCER RESEARCH AND TREATMENT-NATIONALIZATION OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time has come when the government should take immediate action, with a view to the nationalization of the supply of radium.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I do not think 1
owe any apology to the house for undertaking for a short time to draw the attention of hon. members to a question which, I believe, is of real national importance. In order to understand the necessity for the introduction of this resolution, it might be of interest to some of those who are not of the medical fraternity to consider for a short time something of the history of the discovery of radium and of the uses to which it is being put at the present time in medical therapeutics.
During the latter part of the nineteenth century a number of men on the continent of Europe and in Great Britain experimented 
with electricity with the result that about 1895 the so-called X-ray or Roentgen ray was given to the world. The study of X-rays led Mr. Henri Becquerel to study certain radioactive compounds which he discovered in uranium ore. Following Becquerel's studies, Madame Curie and her distinguished husband, Pierre Curie, began the study of pitchblende, which contains uranium ore. Perhaps no more brilliant story in the history of scientific research has been recorded than the history of the discovery of radium through the effort* of Madame Curie and her distinguished husband. They began the study of radium compounds in the year 1896, and late in 1898 they discovered a new compound to which they gave the name of radium. At that time radium was derived from pitchblende ore, which was obtained1 from Austria, then practically the only known source of supply in the world. To-day it requires one ton of the richest pitchblende ore in order to obtain one gramme of radium, the radium being present only in the proportion of one to several million parts of the other metals present. In 1904 the cost of a gramme of radium was $160,000.
Following the discovery of radium, scientists in different parts of the world endeavoured to obtain radium from other ores, with the result that in the United States an ore called camotite was discovered in Colorado, and the Americans began producing radium from car-notite ore. Camotite, however, was very poor in radium content, with the result that the cost of radium was excessive. In order that the house may understand just why radium should be so expensive, let me say that in the ease of camotite, in order to extract one gramme of radium five hundred tons of ore have to be treated. That means the handling of about 2,000 tons of sandstone which is associated with that ore. To extract a gramme of radium it is necessary to 'use 500 tons of chemicals to treat the camotite, and at 'least 1,000 tons of distilled water, and over 1,000 tons of coal, or its equivalent in electrical energy.
About the year 1913, just prior to the war, pitchblende ore was discovered in the Belgian Congo. This ore contained a very high radium content compared with the camotite ore of Colorado or the pitchblende ore of Austria. During the period of the war, not much was done with regard to obtaining new sources of supply, but after the war, about 1921 or 1922, pitchblende was taken in considerable quantity from the Belgian Congo. This pitchblende ore contained about forty times as much radium as the camotite ore of Colorado, and

Radium Supply-Mr. Cotnam
on account of the cheapness of labour in the Congo and the exceeding richness of the ore, the American producers of radium were gradually compelled to contract their business, not being able to carry on against the keen competition from the Congo.
At the .present time, in order to obtain the radium, this pitchblende ore is carried some sixteen hundred miles to the sea from Kanaga in the Belgian Congo. Thence it is transported to Belgium, where it is refined by similar processes to those I have outlined for the treating of carnotite ore. It takes a period of probably six months from the time the ore is mined before even a small quantity of radium can be produced, and even the very richest pitchblende ore at the present time requires at least one ton to give one gramme of radium. That explanation will help to satisfy the minds of those who think that the cost of radium treatment in the past has been excessive. It is due to the very small amount of radium present in these ores, and it is not likely that we shall ever obtain ores which are richer in radium content. Radium is always present even the richest in the uranium compounds in the proportion of only one to two or three million parts.
Following the discovery of radium, it was found that certain radium rays could be used therapeutically with great benefit ;n certain types of disease, and to-day radium has come to be associated in the minds of the public with the treatment of cancer, and rightly so because probably no other therapeutic agent that has been introduced to medical science in this or any other country has obtained in so short a time such a foothold in the treatment of disease.

Hon. gentlemen will notice that whereas tuberculosis was formerly considered and was termed by a very eminent medical man, " the captain of the men of death," that position has been usurped in this country by cancer. From the study that has been made of cancer not only in Canada but all over the world, there seems to be a general opinion that the disease is on the increase and that we must use every effort in our power to cope with this menace to the human race.

Radium Supply-Mr. Cotnam
The history of medicine throughout the whole world records that during the last fifty or seventy-five years medical men have been attacking most of these disease problems with a considerable degree of success by applying to their solution the proper methods. For instance, with the discovery of the bacteriological causes of certain diseases, for which we must give credit to that eminent Frenchman, Louis Pasteur, we find that a great number of diseases that formerly were treated more or less empirically and in the dark are being conquered one by one. We all know in particular the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross) will bear me out in this statement that during the South African war the death rate from typhoid fever was appalling, and yet during the great war, owing to the fact that we knew the exact causation of the disease, we were able to reduce to a minimum the death rate from this cause. The same thing is true of tuberculosis. It was only after the discovery of the actual cause of the disease that we were able by introducing proper methods of sanitation and treatment gradually to master that great menace to the human race. Smallpox has practically been eliminated as one of the world scourges by vaccination. The bubonic plague has also been brought under control. Then with the discovery of the diphtheria bacillus this disease which used to be so fatal to the children of this and other countries has virtually been eliminated; today if diphtheria is treated in time very rarely indeed should it result fatally. Malaria and yellow fever are twm other scourges that scientific research has brought under control, the causation of these diseases having been discovered. We have only to recall the disastrous attempt of that famous French engineer, De Lesseps, to build the Panama canal, to realize how all his carefully prepared plans were frustrated by malaria and yellow fever. Later, of course, we all know that this great engineering project was carried to a successful conclusion by our American friends simply because scientific research enabled them to adopt the proper preventive measures to protect their workmen from these diseases. Infantile paralysis, if taken in hand in time, can be cured. Through the research efforts of our Canadian. Doctor Banting, diabetes has been robbed of its terrors.
What has been accomplished in the cases I have mentioned encourages me to urge that we should make a really formidable attack against cancer which is probably the greatest menace that we have to our national health to-day. Hardly a home or family but what is affected directly or indirectly by the ravages

of this disease. At the present time we do not know the exact causation of cancer. In the past most cancer cases were treated by surgery. To-day, I think it may safely be said that surgery has been superseded by radium in the treatment of certain types of cases; other types are best controlled by a combination of radium and surgery; certain other types can actually be cured by radium. And yet that therapeutic agent has only been known to the scientific world for the comparatively short period of thirty years. Perhaps no other curative agent in such a brief space of time has attained such a position in the treatment of disease as has radium in the treatment of cancer. The treatment of cancer by radium is still in its infancy. Radium in small quantities may be not only useless but even harmful. One great surgeon has said that ten cents worth of radium may do one million dollars' worth of damage. It is a substance that should be employed by men who are experienced in its use, and it should be applied in sufficient quantities to do the work which it is supposed to do. At the present time the cost of treatment by radium is really prohibitive to the average poor man.
The object of this resolution is twofold. In the first place, we should be able to secure an adequate supply of radium; we should be able to place that radium in accessible centres, and it should be placed there in the hands of experienced men, those centres where radium treatment is obtained may become centres for cancer scientific research, and the country that can give us a Banting or a Best may perhaps solve the cancer problem of the world to-day. We are still groping in the dark for a cure for a cancer, and the causation of cancer, and I can conceive of no higher objective in the realm of government in this country than that we should secure cooperation between the federal and provincial Departments of Health. If the federal Department of Health has any function at all, surely this is a place where it should function. I know the time-worn objection will probably be trotted out on this occasion that this is another case of contribution by the federal government, by grace, to the provincial health departments. There is no place to-day in this country where we need so much cooperation as in this matter, the study and care of the national health and happiness of the people, and if the federal Department of Health will cooperate with the provincial departments of health I think some basis can be arrived at whereby we shall have proper handling of this cancer problem. A question such as this cannot be deaLt with from the

Radium Supply-Mr. Cotnam
point of view of the boundary between Manitoba and Ontario, or between Saskatchewan and Alberta. Unfortunately cancer knows no provincial boundaries. It is widespread in this country, and where it is taking such a toll of life surely there could be no greater objective for the federal Department of Health than to devise some means whereby radium could be placed at the disposal of those people who are so unfortunate as to be suffering from this terrible scourge.

on the cancer problem, and I believe the Dominion should take this matter up and that the whole subject should be studied in all its bearings. Canada should not be in the rearguard but rather should be in the vanguard in this movement in the fight against cancer. In France, which was the home of radium, they have already nationalized their supply. They have at the present time fifteen national institutes; the supply of radium is furnished by their central government, and these institutes all cooperate in order to secure the very best results in the treatment of cancer. No man buying radium out of a private income, no ordinary individual, can buy in the quantities which are necessary for effective treatment. As everyone knows, radium can be continually in use and still not deteriorate. Where radium is owned by private individuals there is usually a great deal of waste in the use of the radium itself. In Belgium there is a system of nationalization. Sweden has taken up this subject very actively, and probably some of the best radium work in the world to-day has been done in Sweden. In Australia I understand that their legislative organization is somewhat similar to what we have in Canada, with a federal parliament and provincial legislatures. Last year or the 2419-44
year before they nationalized their supply of radium, and they secured from Great Britain the services of the assistant director of the radium institute in London, who went over to supervise and control the use of their nationalized supply. The director of the radium institute in London was authority for the statement that radium in small quantities, was likely to be ineffective and inefficient. The house can understand, therefore, why it is impossible for ordinary hospitals or private physicians to obtain and have in their control a supply of radium which would be effective in fighting this great cancer menace. It would require at least $40,000 worth for effective treatment.
The proposal that I wish to place before the house is briefly this: that we should establish centres under government control where radium could be obtained in sufficient quantities; that we should have, in the maritime provinces one or two centres; one or two in the province of Quebec; two or three in Ontario; one in each of the prairie provinces, and probably one in British Columbia. That, of course, is a tentative proposal. The thought is that these centres should become primarily cancer research centres; that the men there should thoroughly understand the whole cancer problem, and be in a position to give the very best treatment, and that, radium alone not being sufficient, these institutes could probably be established in existing institutions and be run in cooperation with hospitals.

Of the various forms of cancer for which radium has been tried, none affords a more striking example than cancer of the womb. The number of women who died of this form of cancer in 1926 was 4,409,

As a result we have to go to the Standard Chemical Company of New York and buy radium or the emanations of radium for the treatment of patients in this country.
I want to draw the attention of the house to another fact, and that is that in considering the primary operation of treating a patient with radium or by a major operation, the initial death rate in many forms of cancer runs as high as 10 per cent under the major operation, while with radium it is practically nil. Moreover, the radium treatment lends itself to a greater application because, as every medical man knows, there are comparatively few men so skilled in surgery as to perform the difficult operations that are required for the eradication of carcinoma, while with radium the treatment is relatively simple and the death rate from the initial operation is practically nil. We are told by those who are most skilled and experienced in the use of radium that in many forms of cancer, as the hon. member for North Renfrew has said,

Radium Supply-Mr. McGibbon
radium is much to be preferred to a major operation with the knife, for instance, in all forms of cancer of the tongue, cancer of the uvula, the tonsils, the pharynx or nasal cavities, radium is preferred while in cancer of the cervix uteri, the major operation formerly known as hysterotomy is now no longer performed by the best surgeons. Radium has superseded it because the results have been better. About four years ago in New Orleans I was taken by one of the leading surgeons to the state hospital where they had 2,000 beds, most of which contained two patients At that time he told me he had given up performing hysterotomy for carcinoma, because he had got much better results from radium. His results have been confirmed by the leading doctors of New York and London, so that this instrument, which is comparatively simple in skilled hands and undoubtedly much to be preferred by the patient, has decreased the death rate from carcinoma to an enormous extent, as I shall show a little later.
In addition to that, there is something that is very important, and it is this: once the public understand there is a method of treating carcinoma other than by an operation as understood previously, you will have them appealing to the surgeon much earlier and with less fear, and they will seek advice during that stage of the disease when advice will be most useful to them and also to the surgeon so far as getting results is concerned. I have under my hand a record of some results of Doctor Gray Ward of New York in regard to radium. This was based on the results in the Women's Hospital there. In regard to carcinoma of the uterus or cervix uteri he found 20.1 per cent living at the end of five years and in cases of cancer of the cervix only he found 53.1 per cent living at the end of five years. I only need to appeal to the medical men and surgeons here for confirmation when I say that those results compare very favourably with anything previously recorded in medical literature.
I also have a record of some results by Doctor Hurdon in London. He had 169 cases of cancer of the cervix and 18 cases of cancer of the body, or a total of 187 cases. After five years there were 70 per cent of these still alive, and they were treated with radium. That was taking the operable and inoperable cases together. When he took the operable cases alone he had the astounding figure of 95 per cent still alive after a period of five years.
I pause to put this question to the house: When you have any instrument, no matter
what it is, that will produce such valuable results in a disease that has caused so much death and trouble in the world, is it not something of which the house and the country should take cognizance?
I might for a moment, if time will permit, tell the house what some other countries have been doing, because nearly every country in the world, outside of Canada, is spending a great deal of time on and has a number of institutions devoted entirely to cancer research. That as something which, as I said before, the Department of Health should have been taking into consideration long ago, but I also think sometimes that if any original idea whatever strikes this department, it would have to have something like a shock-absorber to be prevented from being shattered to pieces.
May I read a memorandum by the Minister of Health of Great Britain on cancer of the breast, which is a very common disease in this or any other country, with a very high mortality? I will read it only in part:
The memorandum sets forth the results of the special investigation carried out at Leeds, and contained in the Ministry of Health 1926 reports on public health and medical subjects No. 34. This investigation showed that, with the modern complete operation, 52 per cent of all the patients were alive and well after three years-
That is 52 per cent of cases of cancer of the breast. I have given the facts as to cancer of the cervix and of the body of the uterus, and I have also pointed out that for cancer of the nasal cavities, the tongue, lip et cetera, radium is far superior to surgery. The memorandum continues:
Thirty-nine per cent after five years, and 30 per cent after ten years.
But this is the point I want to impress upon the house:
But if the patients were classed as being in the early, middle and late stages of the disease when operated on, it was found that of the early cases 94 per cent were alive and well after three years.
Let us compare that with the idea that the public have had of this disease in the past.
Of the early cases 94 per cent were alive and well after three years, 95 per cent after five years and 87 per cent at the end of ten years.
I wonder, if we could get that across to the suffiering public, whether it would not hold out a little hope to them and with that hope induce them to appear before their medical or surgical advisers earlier in the stage of the disease so that the treatment might be much more efficacious.

This is another statement I would like to put on Hansard. It reads:
On the average women affected by cancer of the breast have, in the absence of effective treatment. roughly one-sixth of the normal duration of life to look forward to; those subjected to the complete operation during the comparatively early stage of the disease at which the average patient applies for treatment under present unsatisfactory conditions have about one-third of the normal duration to expect; while those so operated upon at an early stage may anticipate approximately two-thirds of the normal after life-time.
We see there the statistical results of early treatment of the disease. It is something that we should make an effort to let the public fully appreciate, especially those poor women who have a cloud hanging over their heads, a cloud of depression that probaibly none of us realizes, and who are suffering the agony of a possible return of their malady.
Let me quote a few comments from Dr. Malcolm Donaldson, of St. Bartholomew's Hospital, London, England. He favours radiation as against hysterectomy for the following reasons:
1.	The negligible mortality due to the . radiation treatment.
2.	The fact that statistics of survival rate in no way inferior in the case of radiation to those following hysterectomy.
3.	By improving the technique of radiation treatment the number of patients who seek advice early will be increased and the results will correspondingly improve.
4.	It will bring into general use radiation treatment for those cases which have passed the possibility of being completely restored to health.
5.	It will encourage the younger generation of gynaecologists to adopt a method of treatment which the greater number will be able to carry out more successfully than Wertheim's operation, recognized as one of the most difficult operations in the whole domain of surgery.
That summarizes the advice that has been given out by that hospital based upon their experience. I should like also to quote :a 'statement of Mr. Chamberlain, then Minister of Health in Great Britain, when attending a lecture on this subject by Lord Moynihan, then Sir Berkeley Moynihan. Mr. Chamberlain was apparently very much alive to the duties of his position. He spoke as follows:
We have come here to-night to take advantage of a unique opportunity-the opportunity of hearing the views of one of our greatest surgeons upon a subject which is of the very first importance and interest to the nation. Of all the diseases known to us none is looked upon with greater repulsion and apprehension than cancer, partly because of its nature, partly because of the mystery which surrounds its origin, but most of all, perhaps, because it

appears to be marching on in a sort of irresistible progress, taking a greater toll of victims from our midst year by year.
I would like the house to note the following:
In 1850 the deaths from cancer were recorded as about 300 per million living; in 1900 as 800 per million, and in 1925 as 1,336 per million, so that in the short space of two generations or less the death rate from cancer appears to have increased fivefold. These figures are the more remarkable when you contrast them with those pertaining to other diseases. Forty years ago the death rate from tuberculosis was four or five times that from cancer; to-day the cancer death rate is about one-third greater than that of tubercidosis. Making allowances for certain qualifications, these figures still justify the general public anxiety and make it necessary that we should use all our resources in fighting this great evil.
I would like the Minister of Health to note that phrase:
We should use all our resources in fighting this great evil.	.
He continues:
In that fight everybody must take part-the ministry of health, the local authorities, the research investigators, the medical profession, and the general public. As Minister of Health I am directel by act of parliament to take measures for the prevention and cure of diseases.
That is what I would like to impress upon the Minister of Health for Canada.
I do not claim to be able to speak on radium myself, but I have had a number of patients treated with it, and I have given much consideration to the subject. I have investigated practically all the statistics that I have been able to find, and I feel that I am in a position to give these facts to the public from my place in this house better perhaps than anywhere else. That has been my principal object in speaking to-night.
As the hon. member for North Renfrew has said, the radium treatment is still in its infancy. A great deal has been learned in the last four years. Some harm was done in the earlier stages of its use through not knowing how to handle it properly, but experience is being gained every day.
One of the things that require serious consideration in the treatment is the dosage. That is one justification for the hon. member for North Renfrew claiming that we should have special hospitals and that the radium treatment should be in the hands of a competent surgeon only. It should go hand in hand with major surgery, as it must, because the major operation is performed first, and then the radium seeds travel along the lympathics and blood vessels so as to attack anything that has

Radium Supply-Mr. McGibbon
escaped the surgeon. That is one reason, I say, why the government would be justified in establishing hospitals for clinical research where nothing else would be done but cancer research, and where patients could go and be treated without cost to themselves, if necessary.
Those are some of the things that have to be considered.
In figuring the dosage the following factors have to be considered: First, the amount of tissue that has to be destroyed in the body. Upon that will depend the amount of radium to be used, and the duration of the treatment. Roughly speaking, 10,000 milligramme hours is the maximum dosage, and about two grammes of radium are required. I do not know if any province in the Dominion of Canada has got that much. The city of Toronto has only half a gramme and as I say, we have to send to the Standard Chemical Company of the United States to get the radium that we require for treatment.
Another factor that enters into the dosage is the resistance of the body to radium treatment.
Another factor is that radium, through radiation, loses about sixteen per cent of its efficacy in the first twelve hours, and that must be considered now that we are getting our radium from New York. We have to consider the time that the radium will be in the mails or *express. We used to gather the emanations from radium in glass; now we gather them in gold or platinum tubes. These are from two to six centimetres long. Some years ago I went through the plant of the Radium Insti-tue in Philadelphia and was shown how the emanations were collected and sealed in glass tubes for distribution throughout the country. To emphasize the security of the investment, I may say that radium loses about 50 per cent of its efficacy after about 5,000 years. So we are pretty safe in investing our money in rradium.
There are one or two other things I want to put on Hansard. Doctor Sampson Handley reports that for icancer of the breast he uses both surgery and radium. The results-which after all are what interest the public-the results, I say, show 48 per cent free at the end of eight years; that is both local and auxiliary recurrence were absent. Then he compares the results of surgery and radium treatment of cancer of the tongue, and reports that when he used surgery the death rate was 10 per cent and the duration of life from 6 to 24 months; while when he used radium his patients were alive and well from four to six years afterwards. As I said before, cancer [DOT]of the oral cavity, the tongue, the lips, the
uvula, ithe pillars of fauces and the buccal cavity responds best to radium. I might go a little further and say that all epitheliomata, that is, cancer of epidermal origin, comes in the same class; that is, radium is preferable to any other line of treatment.
Now, I want to call the attention of the house for a moment or two to what is going on in other parts of the world in the direction of cancer research. In 1922 the ministry of health of Great Britain appointed a departmental .commission to investigate the causation, prevalence and treatment of cancer and to advise the ministry. In 1923 the British empire cancer campaign Started, a voluntary ergniza-tion with headquarters in London. Its object was to correlate and extend all the existing efforts for the cure of cancer. This organization distributes one and a quarter million dollars' worth of radium each year. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is something which I think this country should take note of. When you get a single institution in Great Britain dispensing a million and a quarter dollars' worth of radium each year for the treatment of cancer, those in charge of that institution must think something of radium as a curative agent. In 1923 the League of Nations set up a cancer commission. France has a number of anti-cancerous institutions. If I mistake not, sir, there was another *cancer institution started in London to celebrate the recovery of King George. I am speaking from memory, but I think one individual gave something over half a million dollars to start the institution. In Stockholm they have an institution for the treatment of cancer that was organized way back in 1910. This institution is supported both by the government and the city and has a world wide reputation. Belgium has given a subsidy of a million gold marks for cancer research. The United States have many institutions for the control of cancer. There is the cancer committee in connection with the American Medical Association, also the cancer commission of American public health which was started in 1927, while in Boston they have the Collis B. Huntington Memorial hospital for cancer reasearoh. Sweden, to which I think the member for North Renfrew referred, has recently collected $1,000,000 as a jubilee fund to purchase six grammes of radium for presentation to Kinig Gustav on his seventieth birday. I think Sweden has something like eighteen grammes of radium. *We in Ontario have, I think, less than one half of one gramme.
